name: Patras
title: Patras Ro-Pax Thickness Gauging | Adriatic Ferry UTM
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Patras for Adriatic ro-pax ferries, freight ro-ro ships and cargo vessels: car deck, ramp, ballast tank and hull UTM.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Ro-Pax Ferries and Ships at the Port of Patras
intro: Patras is Greece's western gateway to Italy, and its south port is built around the large ro-pax ferries that link it, often by way of Igoumenitsa, with Ancona, Bari, Brindisi and Venice. These ships carry lorries, trailers, cars and passengers on fixed schedules all year, so their vehicle decks, ramps and tanks work hard and their dockings are planned tightly. Gauging has to fit layovers and refit periods. Technicians are flown in from India for each job and meet the ship at its berth or in the Gulf of Patras.

highlights.p: Adriatic ferries usually spend part of each rotation alongside at Patras between arrival and the next sailing. Deck plating, ramps and voids can be measured in that time, and a broader scope planned for an extended layover or a scheduled lay day.

highlights.h: Freight decks under heavy axle loads
highlights.p: Lorries and unaccompanied trailers make up much of the cargo on these routes. Their weight and constant movement wear vehicle-deck plating, stiffeners and ramp structure, and corrosion under the wear surface is easy to underestimate without measured readings from the actual steel.

Ro-pax ships on regular services to and from EU ports are inspected under EU rules by the host states. Measured data on decks, shell doors, ramps and tanks gives the operator evidence of condition before inspectors and class surveyors come aboard.

port.h: Patras: the ferry port on the Gulf of Patras
p: Patras lies on the northern coast of the Peloponnese, facing the Gulf of Patras, which opens westward to the Ionian Sea and narrows eastward to the strait spanned by the Rio-Antirrio bridge at the entrance to the Gulf of Corinth. Ships reach the port from the Ionian through open water with few navigational constraints, which is part of why the Adriatic ferry lines made it their Peloponnese terminal. Ferry traffic moved from the old harbour in the city centre to a purpose-built south port, with dedicated ro-pax berths, linkspans and large marshalling areas for lorries, while the older harbour serves smaller vessels and other traffic. The motorway network links the port with Athens and with western Greece along the Ionian coast.

The core traffic is ro-pax. Large ferries on routes to Ancona, Bari, Brindisi and Venice carry heavy goods vehicles and trailers moving between Greece and the rest of Europe, together with private cars and passengers, and many call at Igoumenitsa on the way. Demand peaks in summer with holiday traffic, but freight keeps the lines running year-round, so the ships rarely lie idle for long. Most of the fleet is large Greek- or Italian-operated tonnage, some of it built for these routes and some transferred from other European services, and much of it has reached an age where structural condition matters as much as speed or capacity. Other traffic includes general cargo ships at the older quays, yachts in the marina and coastal passenger vessels working the gulf.

Ships waiting for a berth or for orders anchor in the Gulf of Patras off the port, in reasonably sheltered water, although westerly and south-westerly winds blowing in from the Ionian can raise a short sea and interrupt launch transfers. The gulf is generally calm in summer, and the tidal range is negligible. Because the ferries keep schedules, the useful windows for gauging are set by the rotation: the hours alongside at Patras between arrival and departure, any scheduled lay day, and the annual refit or docking, which operators prefer to take outside the summer peak. Away from the ferry berths, cargo ships at the older quays stay for a few days and can be gauged during discharge, while ships at anchor are reached by launch arranged through the agent.

facilities.h: Gauging at the Patras ferry terminals and in the gulf
p: Most Patras gauging takes place on ferries alongside the south port berths. With the vehicles discharged, the lower and main vehicle decks, internal ramps, the stern ramp and its hinges, and the shell door surrounds are accessible, and voids and ballast tanks can be added if the crew can empty and certify them before the next loading. Linkspan landing areas, mooring decks and the steel around lashing points are routinely included. Because time alongside is fixed, the scope is ordered so that the most important structure is finished first and the remainder rolls over to the next call or the refit, without the ferry ever missing a departure.

There is no large ship-repair yard at Patras, so ferries go elsewhere for docking and heavy steel renewal: to the Perama, Salamina and Elefsina yards in Attica, to Chalkida, or to yards abroad chosen by the operator. Gauging at Patras is therefore preparation for the refit as much as a survey in itself. An operator who has measured vehicle decks, tanks and shell framing over several calls can give the yard a firm scope before the ship arrives, which keeps an already short refit on schedule. For cargo ships at the older quays and ships at anchor in the gulf, the work is the familiar afloat kind: holds, hatch covers, deck and ballast tanks as cargo operations and tank preparation allow.
list: South port ro-pax berths: vehicle deck, internal ramp, stern ramp and shell door gauging during layovers between Adriatic sailings
Ferry lay-day berths: longer scopes covering ballast tanks, voids and shell framing from inside
Older harbour quays: hold, hatch cover and deck gauging on general cargo ships during discharge
Gulf of Patras anchorage: condition and pre-purchase gauging by launch on ships waiting for a berth or orders
Attica, Chalkida and overseas yards: where Patras ferries dock for bottom gauging and heavy steel renewal

context.h: Ro-pax inspection rules and the Adriatic ferry fleet
p: Patras is a Paris MoU port, with port state control and harbour supervision by the Hellenic Coast Guard. For the ferries, the more frequent regime is the EU system of inspections for ro-pax ships and high-speed craft in regular service, Directive (EU) 2017/2110, under which the host state inspects each ship before it starts a service and at regular intervals afterwards, including during a scheduled crossing. Hull condition, watertight and weathertight closures, shell doors and vehicle decks are part of what those inspections look at. Ships calling at EU ports also need an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, and the Italy routes fall under the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime.

The age of the fleet makes structural data valuable. Much of the Adriatic ferry tonnage has been in service long enough that its vehicle decks have carried heavy freight on thousands of crossings, its ballast tanks have outlived their original coatings, and its shell doors and ramps have cycled open and shut on every call. Operators facing renewal surveys must decide whether to renew steel, rebuild a deck or replace the ship, and route deployment depends on that answer too. Measured data from Patras layovers, collected over a season, turns a refit from a voyage of discovery into a planned job with a known steel list, and gives the operator firmer ground when a ship is offered for sale or charter.

jobs.p: Patras jobs come mainly from ferry operators, and they are planned around the timetable. The technical department identifies the decks, ramps and tanks that will decide the next refit's steel list, and we spread the measurement across one or more layovers so no sailing is delayed. Cargo ships at the older quays and ships at anchor bring the rest: pre-purchase checks, condition surveys and pre-docking readings. Before each job we confirm with the chief officer which spaces will be free of vehicles and which tanks can be emptied, and we report results area by area so the operator can adjust the next layover's scope. Typical work includes:
list: Main and lower vehicle deck gauging on an Adriatic ro-pax ferry, spread over two layovers at the south port, ahead of its renewal survey.
Magnetic particle testing at stern-ramp hinges and their deck foundations, with ultrasonic gauging of the surrounding plating, on a freight ro-ro ship.
Ballast tank and void-space gauging on a ro-pax ferry during a scheduled lay day, so the refit yard receives a firm steel estimate.
Pre-purchase gauging on a ferry being sold out of the Adriatic trade, covering decks, shell framing from inside and tank boundaries.
Hold and hatch cover gauging on a general cargo ship discharging at the older harbour.

logistics: Athens International Airport is the usual arrival point, with the motorway along the Gulf of Corinth leading west to Patras; Araxos airport, west of the city, has mainly seasonal flights. The south port is a controlled ISPS area, and the ferry operator or the ship's agent arranges passes and boarding with the technicians' details and equipment lists. Each technician needs a Schengen visa issued in India. For refit preparation spread over several calls, we suggest a visa that covers the whole season of layovers rather than a single date.

faqs.q: Can a ferry be gauged during its normal layover at Patras without delaying departure?
faqs.a: Yes, if the scope is matched to the time alongside. Vehicle decks, ramps and accessible voids can be measured once vehicles are off and before loading starts. We agree a priority list with the operator, finish the most important areas first and stop on time, carrying any remaining areas to the next call. Tanks are included only when the crew can empty and certify them within the layover.

faqs.q: Do the EU ro-pax inspections require thickness measurement?
faqs.a: Not as such. The host-state inspections under Directive (EU) 2017/2110 examine the ship's safe operation and condition, including hull, closures and vehicle decks, but thickness measurement is set by class rules and the survey cycle. Operators use gauging to know the state of the structure before inspectors and class surveyors look at it, so any wastage is already planned for repair.

faqs.q: Patras has no drydock. How do your readings help the refit yard?
faqs.a: Ferries from Patras usually dock in Attica, at Chalkida or at a yard abroad. Readings taken at Patras carry the frame and deck references of the thickness measurement plan, so the yard can plan plate, staging and labour, and the class surveyor can see in advance where substantial corrosion lies. If useful, the team can also attend the docking to complete the bottom and shell readings.

faqs.q: Can you work on a ferry that calls at both Patras and Igoumenitsa?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Italy-route ferries call at both ports, and a scope can be divided between them, measuring some decks at Igoumenitsa and the rest at Patras on the same rotation. Both ports can be covered by road during one visit. We coordinate access through the operator, so the work follows the ship rather than the other way round.
